chapters.1: God creates the heavens and the earth in six days, speaking light, sky, land, plants, sun, moon, stars, sea creatures, birds, animals, and finally humans into existence. Man and woman are made in God's image and given charge over the earth and its creatures. On the seventh day God looks over everything he made and calls it very good.
chapters.2: God rests on the seventh day and blesses it. The focus narrows to a detailed picture of creation: God forms the man from dust, breathes life into him, and places him in the Garden of Eden to tend it, forbidding him to eat from the tree of knowledge of good and evil. Finding no suitable companion among the animals, God makes a woman from the man's rib, and the two are joined as husband and wife.
chapters.3: A serpent tempts the woman to eat fruit from the forbidden tree, telling her she won't really die and will gain godlike knowledge; she eats and gives some to her husband. Their eyes are opened, they feel shame and hide from God, and each is confronted and cursed: the serpent to crawl and be at odds with humanity, the woman with painful childbirth and a hard marriage dynamic, the man with hard labor and mortality. God clothes them in animal skins and expels them from Eden.
chapters.4: Adam and Eve's sons Cain and Abel bring offerings to God; God accepts Abel's but not Cain's, and a jealous Cain murders Abel. God confronts Cain, curses him to wander, but marks him for protection. The chapter traces Cain's descendants through several generations, including Lamech and his sons who pioneer livestock herding, music, and metalworking, and closes with the birth of Seth's son Enos, when people begin calling on God's name.
chapters.5: A genealogy traces the line from Adam through Seth down to Noah, giving each man's age at the birth of his named son and his total lifespan, with ages running into the hundreds of years. Enoch stands out because the text says he "walked with God" and was simply taken rather than dying. The chapter ends by introducing Noah and his three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
chapters.6: Human wickedness spreads across the earth, and God decides to wipe out life in a flood because of the violence and corruption everywhere, though Noah is singled out as righteous. God gives Noah detailed instructions for building a large wooden ark with multiple decks, and tells him to bring his family and pairs of every kind of animal aboard to survive the coming flood.
chapters.7: Noah, his family, and the animals enter the ark as God commanded, and the flood begins, with rain falling forty days and underground waters bursting out. The waters rise until they cover even the highest mountains, and every living thing outside the ark perishes. Only Noah and those with him in the ark survive, and the flood continues to cover the earth for 150 days.
chapters.8: The floodwaters gradually recede, and the ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven and then a dove three times to check if the ground is dry; when the dove doesn't return, he knows it's safe to disembark. Noah builds an altar and offers sacrifices, and God promises never again to destroy the earth with a flood, and that the seasons and cycle of day and night will continue.
chapters.9: God blesses Noah and his sons, renews the command to multiply and fill the earth, and gives permission to eat meat while forbidding eating blood and murder. God establishes a covenant never to flood the whole earth again, with the rainbow as its sign. The chapter ends with Noah getting drunk and exposing himself; his son Ham sees this and tells his brothers, leading Noah to curse Ham's son Canaan while blessing Shem and Japheth.
chapters.10: This chapter is a genealogy listing the descendants of Noah's three sons, Japheth, Ham, and Shem, naming the various peoples and nations that came from each line, including figures like Nimrod and the ancestors of Egypt, Canaan, and Assyria. It explains how the earth's nations and languages spread out and divided after the flood.
chapters.11: People gather in Shinar and try to build a city and a tower reaching to heaven to make a name for themselves, but God confuses their languages and scatters them, so the unfinished tower is called Babel. The chapter then gives the genealogy from Shem down to Terah, introducing Abram, his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and the family's move from Ur to Haran.
chapters.12: God calls Abram to leave his homeland for a land God will show him, promising to make him a great nation and a blessing to all peoples. Abram travels to Canaan, builds altars along the way, and later goes to Egypt during a famine, where he tells Pharaoh that Sarai is his sister out of fear; Pharaoh takes her, but God sends plagues until Pharaoh learns the truth and sends them away.
chapters.13: Abram returns from Egypt wealthy, and tension arises between his herdsmen and those of his nephew Lot over grazing land. Abram offers Lot first choice of territory, and Lot picks the fertile Jordan plain near Sodom while Abram stays in Canaan. God then reaffirms his promise to give Abram all the land he can see and to make his descendants countless.
chapters.14: A coalition of eastern kings defeats several Canaanite kings and carries off Lot, who lives in Sodom, along with his goods. Abram leads his men in a night raid, rescues Lot and recovers the stolen property, and on his return is blessed by Melchizedek, the priest-king of Salem, to whom Abram gives a tenth of the spoils. Abram refuses any reward from the king of Sodom for himself.
chapters.15: God reassures Abram, who still has no heir, that his own offspring will be as numerous as the stars, and Abram's faith in this promise is credited to him as righteousness. God formalizes a covenant with Abram through a ritual involving animal sacrifices, foretelling that his descendants will be enslaved for 400 years before returning to possess the land of Canaan.
chapters.16: Since Sarai remains childless, she gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram to bear a child on her behalf, and Hagar conceives. When Hagar then looks down on Sarai, Sarai treats her harshly and Hagar flees into the wilderness, where an angel finds her, promises her son Ishmael will become a great people, and tells her to return and submit to Sarai. Hagar gives birth to Ishmael when Abram is eighty-six.
chapters.17: When Abram is ninety-nine, God renews his covenant, changes his name to Abraham ("father of many nations") and Sarai's to Sarah, and promises that Sarah herself will bear a son named Isaac within the covenant line, even as God also blesses Ishmael with a future nation. God establishes circumcision as the sign of the covenant, and Abraham immediately circumcises himself, Ishmael, and all the males of his household.
chapters.18: Three visitors, including the Lord, appear to Abraham at Mamre; he hosts them generously, and they announce that Sarah, despite being old, will have a son within the year, which makes Sarah laugh in disbelief. The Lord then reveals he intends to judge Sodom and Gomorrah for their wickedness, and Abraham intercedes, bargaining God down to sparing the cities if even ten righteous people can be found there.
chapters.19: Two angels visit Lot in Sodom and warn him of the city's coming destruction after the townsmen try to assault them; Lot, his wife, and two daughters are urged to flee before God rains fire and brimstone on Sodom and Gomorrah. Lot's wife looks back and turns into a pillar of salt, and afterward his two daughters get him drunk and conceive sons by him, becoming the ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.
chapters.20: Abraham again claims Sarah is only his sister while staying in Gerar, and King Abimelech takes her, but God warns him in a dream that she is married and he has not touched her. Abimelech confronts Abraham, returns Sarah along with gifts, and Abraham prays for Abimelech's household, which had been struck with infertility because of the matter.
chapters.21: Sarah finally gives birth to Isaac in Abraham's old age, fulfilling God's promise. Tension between Sarah and Hagar's son Ishmael leads Abraham to send Hagar and Ishmael away into the wilderness, where God provides for them and promises Ishmael will also become a great nation. The chapter closes with Abraham making a peace treaty with Abimelech at Beersheba over a disputed well.
chapters.22: God tests Abraham by telling him to sacrifice his son Isaac on a mountain in Moriah; Abraham obeys as far as binding Isaac on the altar, when an angel stops him and provides a ram instead, and God renews his promise of blessing because of Abraham's obedience. The chapter closes with a short genealogy of Abraham's brother Nahor, including the birth of Rebekah.
chapters.23: Sarah dies at age 127 in Hebron, and Abraham negotiates with the local Hittites to purchase the cave of Machpelah and its field from Ephron as a permanent burial site. He pays the full price in silver and buries Sarah there, securing the first piece of land his family legally owns in Canaan.
chapters.24: Abraham sends his trusted servant back to his homeland to find a wife for Isaac among his own relatives rather than the local Canaanites. At a well, the servant prays for a sign and Rebekah appears, offering water to him and his camels just as he had hoped; her family agrees to the marriage, and Rebekah travels back with the servant to become Isaac's wife, who loves her and is comforted after his mother's death.
chapters.25: Abraham has more sons through his wife Keturah, then dies at 175 and is buried alongside Sarah by Isaac and Ishmael; a genealogy lists Ishmael's twelve sons before his death. Isaac marries Rebekah, who after a long wait bears twin sons, Esau and Jacob, who struggle even in the womb; grown Esau later trades his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew.
chapters.26: During a famine, Isaac settles in Gerar and, like his father before him, claims his wife Rebekah is his sister out of fear, until King Abimelech discovers the truth. Isaac prospers greatly in flocks and crops, causing friction with the Philistines over wells, but eventually reaches a peaceful covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba after God renews his promise of blessing to him.
chapters.27: As Isaac's eyesight fails, Rebekah helps her favorite son Jacob disguise himself as his older twin Esau in order to receive their father's blessing meant for the firstborn. Isaac is deceived and blesses Jacob with prosperity and leadership over his brother; when Esau returns and the trick is discovered, he is furious and plans to kill Jacob, prompting Rebekah to send Jacob away to her brother Laban in Haran.
chapters.28: On his way to Haran, Jacob stops for the night and dreams of a staircase reaching to heaven with angels on it, and God appears, repeating the promises of land and descendants made to Abraham and Isaac and pledging to be with Jacob wherever he goes. Jacob wakes in awe, names the place Bethel, and vows that if God brings him home safely he will worship God as his own and give a tenth of all he has.
chapters.29: Jacob arrives in Haran and meets Rachel at a well; her father Laban welcomes him and Jacob agrees to work seven years to marry Rachel. Laban tricks him into marrying the older sister Leah first, then lets him marry Rachel too after another seven years of labor. Leah, unloved compared to Rachel, bears Jacob four sons—Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah—while Rachel remains childless.
chapters.30: Rachel, desperate for children, gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob to bear sons on her behalf, and Leah does the same with her servant Zilpah, adding several more sons to Jacob's growing family; eventually Rachel herself conceives and bears Joseph. Jacob then strikes a deal with Laban over speckled and spotted livestock as his wages, and through selective breeding methods he grows wealthy with large flocks of his own.
chapters.31: Sensing Laban's growing resentment, Jacob gathers his family and flocks and secretly leaves for Canaan; unknown to Jacob, Rachel steals her father's household idols. Laban pursues and confronts Jacob, accusing him of theft and deception, but after searching fails to find the idols and God warns Laban in a dream not to harm Jacob, the two make a covenant of peace and set up a stone marker before parting ways.
chapters.32: As Jacob nears home, he sends gifts ahead to appease his estranged brother Esau, fearing violence, and divides his camp for safety. That night he wrestles with a mysterious man until daybreak; the man blesses him, renames him Israel ("one who struggles with God"), and Jacob comes away limping but marked by the encounter, naming the place Peniel because he has seen God face to face.
chapters.33: Jacob meets Esau, and to his relief his brother greets him warmly rather than with anger, embracing and weeping with him. Jacob presents his gifts, introduces his family, and the brothers part peacefully, with Esau returning to Seir while Jacob settles near Shechem, buying land and building an altar there.
chapters.34: Shechem, a local prince, rapes Jacob's daughter Dinah and then wants to marry her, prompting marriage negotiations between the two families involving mass circumcision of the men of the city. Dinah's brothers Simeon and Levi use the occasion to deceitfully attack the weakened city, killing all its men and plundering it in revenge for their sister's defilement, troubling Jacob over the danger this brings on his family.
chapters.35: God instructs Jacob to return to Bethel, where Jacob builds an altar, has his household rid themselves of foreign idols, and God confirms his new name Israel along with the covenant promises. On the journey, Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin near Bethlehem, and the chapter lists all twelve of Jacob's sons before recording the death of his father Isaac at an old age.
chapters.36: This chapter is a genealogy tracing the descendants of Esau, also called Edom, including his wives, sons, the chieftains ("dukes") of Edom, the earlier Horite inhabitants of the region, and a list of kings who ruled in Edom before Israel had any king. It establishes the family line and territory of the Edomite nation descended from Esau.
chapters.37: Jacob's favorite son Joseph, now seventeen, angers his brothers with tales of dreams suggesting he will rule over them, deepening their jealousy. The brothers plot against him, eventually selling him to traders bound for Egypt instead of killing him, and they deceive their father Jacob into believing a wild animal killed Joseph, leaving Jacob grief-stricken.
chapters.38: Judah's sons Er and Onan both die for wrongdoing before fathering children with Tamar, Er's widow, so Judah withholds his youngest son from her. Tamar then disguises herself and tricks Judah himself into sleeping with her, becoming pregnant; when confronted, Judah acknowledges his own wrongdoing and that she was more righteous than he, and she bears twin sons, Pharez and Zarah.
chapters.39: Sold into slavery in Egypt, Joseph serves faithfully in Potiphar's household and is blessed by God, rising to oversee the entire estate. When Potiphar's wife tries to seduce him and he refuses and flees, she falsely accuses him of assault, and he is thrown into prison, where God continues to be with him and grants him favor even there.
chapters.40: While in prison, Joseph interprets dreams for two of Pharaoh's officials, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker, telling the cupbearer he will be restored to his position in three days and the baker that he will be executed. Both predictions come true exactly as Joseph said, but the restored cupbearer forgets to mention Joseph to Pharaoh.
chapters.41: Pharaoh has troubling dreams about cattle and grain that none of his wise men can interpret, so the cupbearer finally remembers Joseph, who is brought in and explains that the dreams predict seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine in Egypt. Impressed, Pharaoh puts Joseph in charge of the whole land to prepare for the coming crisis, and Joseph oversees the storage of grain during the plentiful years.
chapters.42: Famine drives Joseph's brothers to Egypt to buy grain, where they unknowingly bow before Joseph, now a powerful official, without recognizing him. Joseph tests them, accuses them of being spies, keeps Simeon as a hostage, and demands they bring their youngest brother Benjamin back with them, stirring guilt among the brothers over how they once treated Joseph.
chapters.43: After much persuasion, Jacob reluctantly allows Benjamin to go to Egypt with his brothers to secure more grain and free Simeon. Joseph welcomes them, treats them to a feast, and seats them by birth order in a way that puzzles them, while secretly showing special favor to Benjamin.
chapters.44: Joseph tests his brothers once more by secretly planting his silver cup in Benjamin's sack, then has his steward accuse them of theft when they are caught; this puts Benjamin in danger of becoming a slave. Judah steps forward and passionately offers himself in Benjamin's place, pleading for the sake of their aged father, showing the brothers' changed character.
chapters.45: Moved by Judah's plea, Joseph can no longer hide his identity and tearfully reveals himself to his brothers, reassuring them that God used their actions for good to preserve life during the famine. He sends them back to bring their father Jacob and the whole family down to Egypt, where Pharaoh grants them the best land to settle in.
chapters.46: Jacob sets out for Egypt with God's reassurance, and the chapter lists by name all the sons, grandsons, and family members who travel with him, totaling seventy persons. Joseph meets his father in Goshen with an emotional reunion, and they plan how to present the family, who are shepherds, to Pharaoh.
chapters.47: Joseph introduces his father and brothers to Pharaoh, who grants them the fertile land of Goshen to live in. As the famine worsens, Joseph manages Egypt's grain supply, eventually acquiring the Egyptians' livestock and land in exchange for food, while Jacob's family thrives; years later, aging Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan rather than Egypt.
chapters.48: As Jacob nears death, Joseph brings his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh to receive a blessing. Jacob adopts them as his own, and in a surprising reversal he gives the greater blessing to the younger Ephraim rather than the firstborn Manasseh, prophesying that Ephraim's descendants will become the greater people.
chapters.49: Jacob gathers all twelve sons and gives each a prophetic blessing or assessment describing the future character and fortunes of the tribe descended from him, notably granting Judah a lasting line of leadership and giving Joseph the richest blessing of abundance. He then instructs them to bury him with his ancestors in the cave of Machpelah in Canaan, and dies.
chapters.50: Joseph has his father Jacob embalmed and leads a large procession back to Canaan to bury him in the family tomb at Machpelah, as promised. After Jacob's death, Joseph reassures his brothers that he holds no grudge against them, recognizing that God turned their evil intentions into good; the book ends with Joseph's own death in Egypt and his request that his bones eventually be carried to the promised land.
